article_title: Causal Modelling of Support Interventions for Student Competency Assessment
citation: Francesca Mangili, Alessandro Antonucci, Rafael Cabañas de Paz. (2026). Causal Modelling of Support Interventions for Student Competency Assessment. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.24632
title: Partially specified structural causal model (PSCM) protocol for educational assessment
description: The article proposes modelling educational tests as partially specified structural causal models in which observable endogenous variables (answers and hint usage) are generated by latent exogenous variables. As the article states, "endogenous variables — students' answers and hint usage — are the observed variables of our model, generated by the latent exogenous variables skill, luck, and help-seeking". Structural equations are elicited from domain experts in purely logical form, and the resulting graph is acyclic by construction, making the model semi-Markovian and ensuring more tractable inference. The framework explicitly supports interventional and counterfactual reasoning beyond associative probabilistic learner models.
requirements: Structural equations must be elicited from a domain expert for each question, identifying the relevant skills and the logical relation between skills, luck, help and answers
constraints: The protocol requires the structural equations to be elicited from experts; exogenous marginal PMFs are typically unavailable and must be recovered by causal EM back-propagation
target_learners: compulsory school students
target_learning_goals: assessment of student competencies
profiling individual student abilities
evaluating effects of support interventions such as hints
examples: Applied to a CAT battery assessment of algorithmic skills with 12 question nodes, two skills (algorithmic competence and autonomy), hint, luck and propensity variables
key_sources: Francesca Mangili, Alessandro Antonucci, Rafael Cabañas de Paz. (2026). Causal Modelling of Support Interventions for Student Competency Assessment. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.24632

article_title: AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning: an RCT introducing a novel research-based design in an authentic educational setting
citation: Kestin, G., Miller, K., Klales, A., Milbourne, T. & Ponti, G. (2025). AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning: an RCT introducing a novel research-based design in an authentic educational setting. Scientific Reports 15:17458. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-97652-6
title: PS2 Pal: a custom AI tutor platform engineered around pedagogical best practices
description: PS2 Pal is a GPT-4-based AI tutoring platform built for undergraduate physics lessons. Its system prompt was engineered to "facilitate active engagement, manage cognitive load, and promote a growth mindset," and because a prompt alone could not reliably scaffold multi-part problems, the platform guides students sequentially through each part of each problem. Prompts were enriched with comprehensive step-by-step answers to guard against hallucinations; 83% of students rated its explanations as good as or better than human instructors'.
requirements: A large language model capable of closely following complex prompts
Expert-crafted, question-specific prompts written by instructors experienced with the content
A carefully structured framework designed to scaffold and guide student interactions
High-quality instructional videos
constraints: Accuracy relied on pre-written answers rather than model-generated solutions
Preparation of system prompts and solutions took significant overhead, and the platform software took several months to develop
target_learners: undergraduate students in introductory physics
target_learning_goals: physics concepts and problem-solving skills at the understanding, applying, and analyzing levels of Bloom's Taxonomy
examples: Students worked through the lesson handout, asking questions and confirming answers with the AI tutor called PS2 Pal

article_title: PsyScore: A Psychometrically-Aware Framework for Trait-Adaptive Essay Scoring and ZPD-Scaffolded Feedback
citation: Wei Xia, Jin Wu, Haoran Shi, Xiangyu Wang, Chanjin Zheng. (2026). PsyScore: A Psychometrically-Aware Framework for Trait-Adaptive Essay Scoring and ZPD-Scaffolded Feedback. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20287
title: PsyScore: a psychometrically-aware framework unifying diagnostic scoring and ZPD-scaffolded feedback through a shared latent ability representation
description: PsyScore couples three modules: a Trait-Adaptive Neural GPCM Scorer that embeds the Graded Partial Credit Model in a BERT-based architecture to estimate latent ability θ; a ZPD-Conditional Feedback Generator that maps θ to instructional strategies via multi-agent fusion; and a Multi-Perspective Evaluation Strategy. The framework's premise is that "modeling student ability within a shared psychometric latent space can unify interpretable scoring and ZPD-aligned feedback", turning AES from summative scoring into formative diagnosis.
requirements: Requires fine-grained analytic trait labels (e.g., Voice, Organization) for trait-adaptive scorer training
Requires heterogeneous LLM agents plus a fusion model for feedback generation
constraints: Multi-agent consensus trades off inference latency, limiting real-time classroom deployment
Simulated revision cannot model motivational dynamics, epistemic trust, or cognitive fatigue
target_learners: K-12 and secondary essay writers across argumentative, source-based, and narrative genres
target_learning_goals: Writing proficiency across multiple traits (content, organization, conventions, voice, etc.)
examples: On ASAP++, the framework's scorer reached QWK 0.747 and its feedback module was evaluated via LLM-judge preference, simulated revision, and a three-expert blind study

article_title: Estimating Learners' Skill Acquisition Without Temporal Information
citation: Ryosuke Nagai, Kyohei Atarashi, Koh Takeuchi, Jill-Jênn Vie, and Hisashi Kashima. (2026). Estimating Learners' Skill Acquisition Without Temporal Information. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20611
title: Pseudo-temporal ordering: inclusion relations among snapshot skill sets as a proxy for learning progression
description: The article proposes a framework in which, absent temporal logs, set-inclusion relations among learners' mastered-skill sets induce a pseudo-temporal axis: a learner whose mastered-skill set is a superset of another's can be viewed as a plausible later state. Learning is modeled as accumulation of expected one-skill increments, so that "a learner's mastered-skill set expands monotonically over time" under a non-forgetting assumption. This supports next-skill prediction from CDM-derived snapshot mastery patterns.
requirements: A predefined mapping between items and skills from cognitive diagnostic models to produce binary mastery patterns
The non-forgetting assumption that once a skill is mastered it remains mastered
constraints: Relies on a non-forgetting assumption; forgetting mechanisms are not incorporated
Evaluated on a restricted real-world subset of learners who attempted all skills
target_learners: Learners in large-scale periodic assessment settings with only snapshot data
target_learning_goals: Predicting the next skill to be acquired to support adaptive instruction
examples: Applied to PISA-style cross-sectional assessment settings where learner data are snapshots rather than temporal traces

article_title: Towards a Theory of When and How Problem Solving Followed by Instruction Supports Learning
citation: Loibl, K., Roll, I. & Rummel, N. (2017). Towards a Theory of When and How Problem Solving Followed by Instruction Supports Learning. Educational Psychology Review, 29, 693–715. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-016-9379-x
title: Initial theory of PS-I: a set of interconnected cognitive mechanisms accounting for when and how problem solving followed by instruction supports learning
description: The article proposes an initial theory of PS-I built on a set of interconnected cognitive mechanisms. The authors state that "The second goal is to identify a set of interconnected cognitive mechanisms that may account for these outcomes" and that "Empirical evidence from PS-I literature is associated with these mechanisms and supports an initial theory of PS-I." The theory explains both positive and negative effects of PS-I implementations: "positive and negative effects of PS-I are explained using the suggested mechanisms." It organizes the review's empirical findings into a mechanism-based explanatory account of the two-phase instructional scheme.
requirements: The theory links mechanisms to empirical evidence from PS-I literature, as the article associates "Empirical evidence from PS-I literature" with the mechanisms
constraints: The article labels it an "initial theory of PS-I"
target_learners: learners in PS-I implementations (e.g., mathematics and statistics students in the reviewed studies)
target_learning_goals: conceptual and procedural learning outcomes addressed by PS-I approaches
examples: The review associates empirical evidence from PS-I studies with the mechanisms and uses them to explain positive and negative effects.

citation: Loibl, K., Roll, I. & Rummel, N. (2017). Towards a Theory of When and How Problem Solving Followed by Instruction Supports Learning. Educational Psychology Review, 29, 693–715. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-016-9379-x
title: Taxonomy of PS-I implementations: mapping designs by commonalities and differences, with Productive Failure and Invention as prominent examples
description: The article organizes the landscape of PS-I approaches by mapping implementations and identifying shared and differing design features. It states the first goal is "to map the landscape of different PS-I implementations, to identify commonalities and differences in designs, and to associate the identified design features with patterns in the learning outcomes." Productive Failure and Invention are named as often cited examples: "Two often cited examples of instructional approaches following the PS-I scheme include Productive Failure and Invention." The taxonomy serves as the organizing framework for the review's outcome analysis.
requirements: Design features must be identifiable across implementations so they can be associated with learning outcome patterns
constraints: Wording differences across conditions that are natural (e.g., invent a formula versus solve using a formula) are not counted as design confounds, per the article's notes
target_learners: designers and researchers of PS-I instruction; learners in problem-solving-first settings
target_learning_goals: preparing learners for learning from subsequent instruction
examples: Productive Failure and Invention are the two often cited PS-I examples the review uses to illustrate the scheme.

article_title: Towards a Theory of When and How Problem Solving Followed by Instruction Supports Learning
citation: Loibl, K., Roll, I. & Rummel, N. (2017). Towards a Theory of When and How Problem Solving Followed by Instruction Supports Learning. Educational Psychology Review, 29, 693–715. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-016-9379-x
title: PS-I lesson structure: an initial problem-solving phase followed by an instruction phase
description: The article defines PS-I as a class of learning approaches combining two phases: "an initial problem-solving phase followed by an instruction phase (PS-I)." This two-phase structure is the reusable lesson-level pattern that Productive Failure and Invention instantiate. The pattern's effectiveness depends on how the phases are designed, with the review showing the instruction phase must feature contrasting cases or build on student solutions. The pattern orients learners before canonical instruction is provided.
requirements: A genuine initial problem-solving phase must precede the instruction phase
The instruction phase must implement contrasting cases or build on student solutions to foster learning
constraints: PS-I without the identified design features is not associated with learning gains in the review
target_learners: K-12 and higher-education students in domains such as mathematics and statistics
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding and preparation for future learning from instruction
examples: Productive Failure and Invention are named by the article as often cited instructional approaches following the PS-I scheme.

citation: Nicola Fuchs-Schündeln, Dirk Krueger, Alexander Ludwig, and Irina Popova. (2020). The Long-Term Distributional and Welfare Effects of Covid-19 School Closures. NBER Working Paper 27773. http://www.nber.org/papers/w27773
title: PSID Child Development Supplement test-score distribution as the calibrated initial human capital endowment of children
description: The article calibrates children's innate ability (initial human capital) distribution from test scores in the PSID Child Development Supplement surveys I-III, merged with the PSID. The sample leaves "4393 observations (2419 children) for the three waves of the survey," using the letter-word test score relative to the group average as a proxy for initial human capital across six child types defined by parental marital status and education. The authors state this poses no causal link between parental education and children's characteristics; the scores only proxy the initial joint distribution.
requirements: Merging the CDS survey waves with the PSID and restricting to children whose caregivers are the household head and spouse with at least one biological parent
constraints: The test scores are explicitly a proxy, not a causal link between parental education and children's characteristics

citation: Iva I. Hrastinski, Ana M. Bonetti, Mladen A. Hedjever. (2023). Relationship between auditory processing skills and academic achievement of elementary school children. Specijalna edukacija i rehabilitacija, 22(2), 95-116. https://doi.org/10.5937/specedreh22-37415

article_title: Learning the control-of-variables strategy through self-generated and vicarious errors: the mediating roles of affect, motivation, cognitive load, and error awareness
citation: Hämmerle, L., Kuhlmann, S. L., Krause-Wichmann, T., & Möller, A. (2026). Learning the control-of-variables strategy through self-generated and vicarious errors: the mediating roles of affect, motivation, cognitive load, and error awareness. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09822-2
title: PS-I error-based learning materials on thermal insulation (wool vs. down) with four condition variants
description: Worksheet-based learning materials developed by the research team, based on prior work by Schmidt (2016), in which "students worked on three experiments in total throughout the PS- and I-phases." The materials taught the CVS by "having them compare the insulating capacity of wool and down," with four PS-phase variants: planning and conducting an experiment (self-generated errors), analyzing two erroneous experiments with a checklist (vicarious errors), both (combination), or analyzing two correct experiments (no-errors). An instruction phase followed with a correct experiment, CVS explanation, and error-reflection tables. Materials were piloted with n = 65 students and provided as translated online material.
requirements: Pre-trained pre-service teacher pairs supported delivery; materials were designed to be primarily self-explanatory
A filler task was added for vicarious and no-errors groups to ensure comparable session durations
constraints: The term "error" refers exclusively to violations of the CVS; experiments with errors unrelated to CVS led to exclusion from analysis
Delayed-test data were excluded due to COVID-19 school lockdowns
target_learners: 7th- and 8th-grade middle school students in an urban region of Austria
target_learning_goals: designing unconfounded experiments by systematically manipulating the independent variable while holding other variables constant
examples: Vicarious-errors students analyzed erroneous experiments containing five CVS-errors each, informed that errors existed but not how many, using a checklist to document experimental variables

title: Common acceptability thresholds for psychometric evidence in education research (review Table 1)
description: The review assembles a framework of psychometric indicators and their common acceptability thresholds in educational research, covering content validity, structural validity, internal consistency, reliability, and criterion validity. For example, it lists "RMSEA < .06; CFI > .95; TLI > .95" for confirmatory factor analysis, internal consistency and test–retest/inter-rater correlations at ≥ .70, diagnostic accuracy at "Sensitivity ≥ .90; Specificity ≥ .70", and criterion correlations at ≥ .60. Tools were rated Acceptable, Mixed, or Low against these thresholds.

Gold Standard measurement tools as reference for criterion validity evaluations
constraints: Gold Standard measurement tools are infrequently available in many countries and cultures in mathematical learning and development research, per the review

citation: Verhoeven, M., Poorthuis, A. M. G., & Volman, M. (2019). The Role of School in Adolescents' Identity Development. A Literature Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-018-9457-3
title: Psychosocial perspective: identity development as exploration and commitment processes
description: The review describes the psychosocial perspective, focused on internal psychological processes, in which "two key stages in the identity development of adolescents are distinguished: exploration and commitment." Exploration involves inquiring into new interests and trying out activities to learn what values and goals one deems important; commitment involves making durable life decisions about education, profession, and worldview. Eight reviewed articles adopted this perspective, favoring large-scale quantitative survey studies of identity stage.

constraints: Scholars adopting this perspective are generally concerned with the process of identity development rather than the content of specific identity dimensions

examples: Survey studies in the review examined the effect of educational characteristics such as education level on the identity stage adolescents find themselves in

article_title: Age norms of psycho-motor capacity.
citation: Wallin, J. E. W. (1915). Age Norms of Psycho-Motor Capacity. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://search.worldcat.org/search?q=Age+Norms+of+Psycho-Motor+Capacity
title: Age norms of psycho-motor capacity and the psycho-motor versus motor test distinction
description: The article defines a normal age norm of psycho-motor capacity as the average quantitative or qualitative score made by normal children of a given chronological age when incited to best effort on a task requiring both muscular movement and "the ability to make the basic intellectual analyses and comparisons." It distinguishes motor tests, which depend primarily on neuro-muscular qualities, from psycho-motor tests, which also demand sensory discrimination, association, memory for relationships, and adaptation to novel situations. Psycho-motor tests are held more valuable for grading mental development because they measure intelligence as well as motor ability.
requirements: Norms must be based on selected groups of normal children, since norms from unselected groups would likely be too low because there are more subnormal than supernormal children.
constraints: The author acknowledges it is impossible to draw an absolutely fixed and sharp line between motor and psycho-motor tests.
target_learners: children of chronological ages two to seventeen
children of varying ability levels including bright, average, dull, feeble-minded, and epileptic
target_learning_goals: assessment of mental capacity and psycho-motor development
examples: The modified Seguin form board (Stoelting's Catalogue Number 78,002), requiring discrimination of ten detached insets, association of forms with recesses, memorization of locations, and quick accurate insertion.

article_title: The Psychopathology of Every-day Life.
citation: Mayer, H. (1911). The Psychopathology of Everyday Life. American Journal of Psychology, 22, 477-527. https://www.jstor.org/stable/1412853
title: Psychoanalytic account of everyday errors: an unconsciously operative repressed wish conditions slips and failures
description: The article presents a psychoanalytic explanatory framework in which everyday imperfections of mental functioning — "slips of the tongue, slips of the pen, symptomatic acts, certain failures to perceive or to remember, as well as false perceptions and false recollections" — are conditioned by an unconsciously operative repressed wish, whether directly or indirectly. The framework denies that such acts are purposeless, holding instead that determinism prevails in mental operations, and links these minor errors to the mechanism of more serious pathological disturbances.
requirements: Interpretation of an error requires uncovering the unconscious motive or repressed wish assumed to condition it
constraints: The account is presented as a psychoanalytic interpretation rather than an experimentally tested result
target_learners: adults reflecting on their own mental functioning
target_learning_goals: understanding the determinants of everyday errors of perception, memory, and action
examples: The review enumerates the deficiencies covered: slips of the tongue, slips of the pen, symptomatic acts, failures to perceive or remember, and false perceptions and recollections.

article_title: Do Spanish-English bilingual children outperform monolingual English-speaking children on executive function tasks in early childhood? A propensity score analysis.
citation: Goodrich, J. M., Koziol, N. A., Yoon, H., & Leiva, S. (2019). Do Spanish-English Bilingual Children Outperform Monolingual English-Speaking Children on Executive Function Tasks in Early Childhood? A Propensity Score Analysis. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.apa.org/pubs/journals/edu
title: Propensity score matching design with 48 covariates and a simulation-based sensitivity analysis for the bilingual advantage question
description: The study's methodological artifact is a comprehensive propensity score matching analysis of ECLS-K:2011 data, in which "a total of 48 child- and school-level covariates were included in the propensity score model," spanning demographics, health-related factors, parent-child engagement, and school-level factors. constraints: Causal inference about early bilingualism is described as unattainable because early bilingualism is not a manipulable variable; the analysis estimates an average controlled difference instead
The article notes it could not account for cultural heterogeneity among Spanish-speaking populations
target_learners: U.S. kindergarten children (bilingual Spanish-English and monolingual English)
target_learning_goals: executive function outcomes in early childhood
examples: Matching yielded 252 bilingual-monolingual pairs; the sensitivity analysis simulated an unobserved confounder based on SES, the covariate with the largest pre-match SMDs

article_title: Do processing patterns of strengths and weaknesses predict differential treatment response?
citation: Miciak Jeremy, Williams Jacob L., Taylor W. Pat, Cirino Paul T., Fletcher Jack M., Vaughn Sharon. (2016). Do Processing Patterns of Strengths and Weaknesses Predict Differential Treatment Response? Journal of Educational Psychology, 108(6), 898-909. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000096
title: Processing strengths and weaknesses (PSW) approaches to LD identification, operationalized by the XBA and C/DM methods
description: PSW methods operationalize a cognitive discrepancy approach to LD identification based on identifying an intraindividual pattern of processing strengths and weaknesses. The XBA approach "utilizes a series of normative comparisons to identify deficient and normal academic and cognitive abilities," requiring an achievement deficit, a normal cognitive profile, and a theoretically related cognitive deficit. The C/DM instead "calculates difference scores across a number of cognitive and achievement tests and compares these difference scores against computed critical values," requiring concordance between achievement and cognitive deficits and discordance with a cognitive strength. Both are aligned with CHC theory in this study.
requirements: Requires a comprehensive psychoeducational assessment battery covering the seven CHC broad cognitive abilities plus reading, administered individually by a trained examiner

article_title: Self-perceptions as mechanisms of achievement inequality: evidence across 70 countries
citation: Hofer, S. I., Heine, J.-H., Besharati, S., Yip, J. C., Reinhold, F., & Brummelman, E. (2024). Self-perceptions as mechanisms of achievement inequality: evidence across 70 countries. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-023-00211-9
title: Psychological affordances account: environments act as 'fertile soil' determining whether self-perceptions translate into achievement
description: The article draws on the psychological affordances account, in which self-perceptions are 'seeds' that only influence behavior in environments that afford that behavior — 'a fertile soil in which these seeds can grow'. Self-perceptions are defined as children's mental representations and evaluations of themselves, often taking the form of personal theories that structure experience. The account explains why the competency and fear-of-failure associations with achievement were stronger in higher-social-mobility countries, with environments that 'afford' growth mindsets conveying that children can improve through effort and dedication.
requirements: A country context that affords acting in line with beneficial self-perceptions (higher social mobility in this study's analyses)
constraints: The account was tested with cross-sectional, correlational PISA 2018 data; causal conclusions are not permitted and b-path estimates may contain reverse effects from achievement to self-perceptions

target_learning_goals: Reading achievement
reduction of socioeconomic achievement inequality
examples: Metaregressions across 57 countries showed the competency a-path (b = 0.045), b-path (b = 5.647), and indirect effect (b = 1.952) were stronger in countries with higher social mobility

citation: Lehto Tuomas MSc, Oinas-Kukkonen Harri PhD. (2011). Persuasive Features in Web-Based Alcohol and Smoking Interventions: A Systematic Review of the Literature. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3222186/

citation: Baker, R. (2016). The Effects of Structured Transfer Pathways in Community Colleges. Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis. https://doi.org/10.3102/0162373716651491
title: Psychic costs of complex decision-making as a barrier to community college persistence
description: The article draws on human capital theory and behavioral economics to explain how community college organizational structures impose psychic costs on students. The theory frames structured interventions like ADTs as reducing these psychic costs by simplifying choice environments.
requirements: The framework assumes that students respond to perceived costs and benefits rather than objective ones, and that structural complexity is a meaningful source of those perceived costs.
constraints: The article notes that the consequences of increased structure are not always clear and that some students might be turned off by having fewer curricular choices.

title: Psychosocial needs of university students as a six-factor construct
description: The article defines and organizes university students' psychosocial needs as a multifaceted construct: "we define psychosocial needs as their desire or requirement to receive help or support for their psychological, social, and emotional well‐being." It hypothesizes six factors — academic, financial, family, friend, practical and emotional support — all covarying positively, which the authors take as evidence the factors measure a similar higher-order psychosocial needs construct. The framework extends Tinto's academic and social integration model by adding financial, practical and emotional need dimensions. The authors also argue family support buffers stressors while friend support normalizes circumstances.

constraints: Higher-order structure was not tested in this study
The practical needs factor was the weakest in reliability and loading strength
target_learners: Undergraduate university students
target_learning_goals: Understanding which psychosocial supports relate to student well-being, distress and academic performance

title: Perceived Stress Scale-10 (PSS-10): 10-item stress measure used for screening, outcome measurement, and follow-up
description: The Perceived Stress Scale-10, developed by Cohen and colleagues, is "a short and easy-to-use scale for measuring individual stress levels," with items measuring "the extent to an individual adjudges their life situations as being stressful in the previous month." It has 10 items rated 0 (never) to 4 (very often), yielding scores from 0 to 40, with higher scores indicating higher stress. The study used it to screen for high stress at baseline, to measure outcomes at post-test and 3-month follow-up, and reported a study reliability of Cronbach α of 0.87.

constraints: Self-administered measure vulnerable to self-reporting bias and to practice effects when used repeatedly, as the authors state in their limitations

target_learning_goals: measurement of perceived stress levels as an outcome of stress management interventions

title: Case-based web-based e-learning module on antibiotic prescribing (Pscribe, endocarditis case)
